title: Preface
content:
Preface Number Systems: From 
N to 
R ended with the real numbers as a complete ordered field. Analysis on the Real Line starts from the axioms of such a field and proves its first limit theorems at once. This volume supplies the working tools that analysis uses on every page without stopping to prove them: inequalities and finite sums, real functions and their graphs, coordinates and vectors in 
R^n, lines, convex sets and isometries, the complex numbers and the plane they form, and distances in the general form of a metric. Who it is for. The reader we have in mind has worked through Logic and Proof, Sets and Functions and the main line of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, or has their habits from elsewhere. Much of the material is familiar in outline from school; what is new is that every rule is proved from the axioms of a complete ordered field, and that nothing is used before it is proved. What it covers. The volume is being written. Its finished chapter is: ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Chapter Title What it does ----------------------- ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 Complex Numbers 
C as pairs of real numbers, proved a field containing 
R; conjugate, modulus and the triangle inequality; square roots and the quadratic formula; why 
C has no order; polar form, De Moivre’s formula and the roots of unity ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Six chapters are planned around it, in this reading order: Inequalities, Finite Sums, and Real Powers; Real Functions and Their Graphs; Coordinates and Vectors in 
R^n; Lines, Convexity, and Isometries of 
R^n; then Complex Numbers; then Rotations, Angles, and the Complex Plane and Metrics and Norms. When they are added, the chapters will be renumbered in that order. How to read it. Every section has Quick checks with folded answers; answer each one before you unfold it. The exercises of a section come in three groups, A to check understanding, B for practice and C to go deeper, and the last section of each chapter adds R items that reach back to earlier chapters. A chapter’s opening page lists what it needs, with links, and the time it takes. Second-reading folds hold edge cases and longer justifications. They can stay closed on a first reading, but they are not optional, since later proofs may use what they contain. One borrowed fact. This volume does not define cosine, sine or \pi: defining them needs limits and power series, which belong to analysis. Section 1.5 states five facts about them, numbered (T1)–(T5), as an assumption, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 10 proves them. They are used only for polar form and for the roots of complex numbers in Sections 1.5 and 1.6, and each proof that uses one names it. Time. Chapter 1 takes about 25 hours on the core track and about 35 hours for everything. What comes next. Analysis on the Real Line uses this volume from its second chapter on. Algebraic Preliminaries takes the complex numbers of Chapter 1 as its main example and builds fields, groups and polynomials on them, ending with the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. The linear algebra volumes, beginning with Spaces and Maps, use the complex numbers throughout.

title: Complex Numbers
content:
Complex Numbers No real number squares to -1: in an ordered field a non-zero square is positive (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), so x^2 + 1 = 0 has no solution in 
R. The usual remedy, “invent a symbol i with i^2 = -1”, leaves open why such a symbol is safe when “a number z with 0 \cdot z = 1” is not. This chapter does not invent anything. It takes pairs of real numbers, objects the reader already trusts, adds them coordinate by coordinate, and multiplies them by the one formula that i^2 = -1 would force. Then it checks, law by law, that nothing breaks: the complex numbers 
C form a field in the sense of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2, and they contain 
R as the pairs (a, 0). Every later volume that computes with complex numbers, from inner products in linear algebra to roots of unity in algebra, starts from this field. Two habits of 
R do not survive the passage. No order on 
C is compatible with its arithmetic, and no choice of “the” square root of each complex number keeps the rule \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{xy}. One new habit takes the place of order: measure a complex number by its modulus, a non-negative real, and compute with \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u}, which is algebra. The first four sections need nothing but the real numbers, and they reach far: division, the triangle inequality, and square roots and the quadratic formula without a single angle. The picture of multiplication as a turn and a stretch does need angles, and angles need cosine and sine, which belong to analysis. The chapter borrows exactly five facts about them, says so in one place, and derives everything else from those five: the familiar special values, De Moivre’s formula, the n different n-th roots of every non-zero complex number, and the roots of unity. It ends with a look ahead at the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, which Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 5 proves without the borrowed facts. What you need. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R above all, and in it chiefly Chapters 2, 4 and 6. From its Chapter 5: the real numbers as a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:def-complete-ordered-field), the standing setting of the whole chapter. From its Chapter 6: square roots of non-negative reals, existing and unique (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), which define the modulus in Section 1.2 and build complex square roots in Section 1.4; the uniqueness of the complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-cof-uniqueness), which lets Section 1.5 carry the borrowed facts over to our 
R; the automorphism theorem (@fd3:thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity), used in the solution of review exercise R1 and compared there with the two such maps of 
C; and the cube roots of its Exercise B2 of Section 6.2 (@fd3:exr-measuring-by-rationals-b2), whose method Section 1.6 runs for every exponent. From its Chapters 2 and 3: the axioms of a field and of an ordered field and their rules (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:def-ordered-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules), used on nearly every page; the finite ring that cannot be ordered (@fd3:exm-finite-ring-not-orderable), compared with in Section 1.4; and the gap at \sqrt 2 in 
Q (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two), which shows in Section 1.2 why the modulus needs completeness. From its Chapter 4: the rules for fractions in a field (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules), the absolute value of an ordered field (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field), which the modulus extends and whose triangle inequality Section 1.3 reproves by a new route, and the natural numbers and powers in an ordered field (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field); a remark of Section 1.4 recalls its exercise on fields with a square root of -1 (@fd3:exr-rules-and-absolute-value-c1). From its Section 2.5: division with remainder, divisibility and parity in 
Z (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers, @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd), in Exercise B1 of Section 1.1 and in Sections 1.5 and 1.6. From its Chapter 1: the citing rule by which induction and recursion apply to 
N (@fd3:cor-omega-identification), and the laws of powers in 
N (@fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity), compared with in Section 1.1. From Sets and Functions: ordered pairs, Cartesian products and injective maps, Chapter 1 (@fd2:def-ordered-pair, @fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:def-injective); divisibility, Section 1.1 (@fd2:def-divides); the recursion theorem, powers and finite sums, Section 3.3 (@fd2:thm-recursion, @fd2:def-power, @fd2:prp-power-laws, @fd2:def-sum-product), whose recursions Section 1.1 reuses in any commutative ring; finite sets, Section 4.1 (@fd2:def-finite), for counting n-th roots; and congruence modulo n and the classes 
Z/n, Section 5.2 (@fd2:def-congruence, @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic, @fd2:prp-integers-mod-n), in Exercise C2 of Section 1.4 and in review exercise R2. From Logic and Proof: induction, Chapter 4 (@fd1:ax-induction); the contrapositive, Chapter 2 (@fd1:prp-contrapositive), in Exercise B3 of Section 1.1; and the catalogue of what a proof may not do, Chapter 8 (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), in the proof-ordering and find-the-error exercises of Sections 1.4 and 1.6. Section 1.4 also proves the complex square roots that Logic and Proof, Section 7.1 took as a school fact. Nothing from linear algebra is used, and nothing from analysis before the box of borrowed facts in Section 1.5. Which real numbers. The chapter builds 
C on the real numbers of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5, whose elements are classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@fd3:def-reals-cauchy-classes). No proof looks inside a real number: every step uses only that 
R is a complete ordered field. By the uniqueness theorem of that volume’s Chapter 6 (@fd3:thm-cof-uniqueness), any complete ordered field would give the same 
C, up to the one isomorphism between the two fields. What this chapter borrows. Everything in Sections 1.1–1.4, and in Section 1.5 up to its box of borrowed facts, is proved from the real numbers. From that box on, five facts (T1)–(T5) about \cos, \sin and \pi are used without proof: the circle identity, the addition formulas, where the cosine equals 1, that every point of the unit circle is reached, and the sign of the sine on the first half turn. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 10 defines the two functions and the number and proves the five facts. No other fact about cosine and sine is used, and the results that rest on the five say so in their dependency ledgers. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Complex Numbers as Pairs of Reals.

R with the product that i^2 = -1 would force; the real numbers inside 
C as the pairs (a, 0), which makes a + bi honest notation and i^2 = -1 a computation; a product with one sign changed, which has zero divisors; the laws of arithmetic, which make 
C a commutative ring with 1 
e 0; powers and their laws in any commutative ring; and the factorization of z^n - w^n. - Conjugate, Modulus, and Division. The conjugate and the modulus, a non-negative real square root and the place where the completeness of 
R enters; the modulus as an extension of the absolute value of 
R; the rules for conjugate and modulus, with \abs{zw} = \abs{z}\abs{w} proved by squaring; the inverse \conj{z}/\abs{z}^2 of a non-zero z; the theorem that 
C is a field in which 
R is closed under the field operations; and division by the conjugate of the denominator. - The Triangle Inequality. Why the trapping proof for ordered fields cannot run in 
C; comparing squares of non-negative reals; real and imaginary parts at most the modulus; the triangle inequality, by expanding \abs{z + w}^2 and recognizing the cross term as a real part; and three variants: the reverse inequality, the inequality for n terms, and a lower bound for the modulus of a sum. - Square Roots, Quadratic Equations, and the Missing Order. An explicit formula for a square root of a complex number, built from two real square roots, and the count of exactly two square roots of every non-zero number; the quadratic formula with complex coefficients; the proof that no order makes 
C an ordered field; and why no choice of square roots keeps the product rule \sqrt{z}\sqrt{w} = \sqrt{zw}. - The Unit Circle and Polar Form. The unit circle 
T, closed under products and inverses, and every non-zero number as a length times a direction in exactly one way, all without angles; the five borrowed facts about cosine and sine; e^{i	heta} as an abbreviation for \cos	heta + i\sin	heta, multiplication as “multiply moduli, add angles”, and polar form, unique up to a multiple of 2\pi in the argument; De Moivre’s formula; and the values of cosine and sine at \pi/6, \pi/4, \pi/3, \pi/2 and \pi, derived from the five facts. - Higher Roots, Roots of Unity, and a Look Ahead. The unique non-negative n-th root of a non-negative real, constructed as a supremum; exactly n solutions of z^n = c for every non-zero c, listed by polar form; the roots of unity, the set \mu_n, and the sums of their powers; a look ahead at the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra; the conjugate of a solution of an equation with real coefficients as a second solution; and review exercises on the maps of 
C to itself that respect sums, products and 1 and send 
R into

Z/n
Z and \mu_n, on the triangle inequality of an ordered field, and on the equation \conj{z} = z^2. Named moves - Compare real and imaginary parts. One equation between complex numbers is two equations between real numbers: for real a, b, c, d, a + bi = c + di if and only if a = c and b = d. It is named in Section 1.1, where it proves the laws of arithmetic; Section 1.4 uses it to turn w^2 = z into two real equations, and Section 1.5 to turn e^{i	heta} = 1 into \cos	heta = 1 and \sin	heta = 0. The warning of Section 1.1 marks the hypothesis it needs: the four numbers must be real. Exercise C1 of Section 1.1 proves the same uniqueness of parts in any field that contains 
R and a square root of -1. - Square the modulus. The modulus is a square root, and square roots do not expand; its square \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u} is a product, and products do. So square, expand with conjugates, bound or compare the real numbers that appear, and take the non-negative square root back, which is legitimate because non-negative reals compare as their squares do. Section 1.2 uses it first, for \abs{zw} = \abs{z}\abs{w}; Section 1.3 names it and runs it in full for the triangle inequality. Z. It is named in Section 1.5, after the multiplication theorem, and gives De Moivre’s formula there; Section 1.6 uses it to solve z^n = c and to count the solutions. title: 1.1 The Complex Numbers as Pairs of Reals
content:
The Complex Numbers as Pairs of Reals The equation x^2 + 1 = 0 has no real solution. In an ordered field every square is non-negative (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) for a non-zero element, and 0^2 = 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so x^2 + 1 \ge 0 + 1 = 1 > 0 for every real x (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), (e)). For most of school mathematics this gap is harmless. Later volumes cannot live with it: the linear-algebra volumes meet real matrices, such as a rotation of the plane, whose most useful data are not real numbers. This section builds the complex numbers, the number system that closes the gap, and proves that they obey the familiar laws of arithmetic. Standing setting. Throughout the chapter, 
R is the complete ordered field built in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5 (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). In particular 
R is a field in the sense of @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, and every rule that book proved for ordered fields holds in it. No proof below looks inside a real number. Letters a, b, c, d, e, f, x, y stand for real numbers, and z, w, u, v for complex numbers, unless we say otherwise. Building the new numbers The quick way to introduce complex numbers is to say “invent a symbol i with i^2 = -1 and compute as usual”. That raises a fair worry. How do we know that such a symbol does not lead to a contradiction, the way “invent a number z with 0 \cdot z = 1” does? The answer is to build the new numbers out of objects we already trust: pairs of real numbers. Here is the recurring expression that suggests the definition. If we pretend i^2 = -1 and expand, we get (a + bi)(c + di) = ac + adi + bci + bd\, i^2 = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i . So a “number a + bi” is really the pair (a, b), and the product should be the pair (ac - bd, ad + bc). We take this formula as the definition, so nothing is pretended. A complex number is a pair of real numbers, multiplied as if i^2 = -1. [Complex Numbers] The set of complex numbers is 
C \coloneqq 
R^2 = 
R 	imes 
R = \{ (a, b) : a, b \in 
R \} , the Cartesian product of @fd2:def-cartesian-product, with addition and multiplication defined for all (a, b), (c, d) \in 
C by  egin{aligned} (a, b) + (c, d) &\coloneqq (a + c, \; b + d) , \ (a, b)(c, d) &\coloneqq (ac - bd, \; ad + bc) . \end{aligned} We write i \coloneqq (0, 1). For z = (a, b) \in 
C, the real part of z is \operatorname{Re} z \coloneqq a and the imaginary part of z is \operatorname{Im} z \coloneqq b. In words: addition is coordinate by coordinate, as for points of the plane. Multiplication is the formula found by expanding. Both right-hand sides are pairs of real numbers, computed with the operations of 
R, so both operations are functions 
C 	imes 
C 	o 
C. The point i is the point one unit up the vertical axis. The real part and the imaginary part of z are its two coordinates, and both are real numbers. There is nothing to check for well-definedness: a pair determines its coordinates, by the characteristic property of ordered pairs (@fd2:def-ordered-pair), (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c 	ext{ and } b = d . In the language of the definition: two complex numbers z and w are equal if and only if \operatorname{Re} z = \operatorname{Re} w and \operatorname{Im} z = \operatorname{Im} w. So one equation between complex numbers is two equations between real numbers. This is the first named move of the chapter, compare real and imaginary parts, and the proofs of @prp-reals-embed-complex and @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws below rest on it. The equation that motivated everything is now a computation: i \cdot i = (0, 1)(0, 1) = (0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1, \; 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0) = (-1, 0) . To read the right-hand side as “-1”, we have to see the real numbers inside 
C. The real numbers inside the complex numbers The real number a should be the point (a, 0) on the horizontal axis. Before we write a for (a, 0), we check that nothing is lost: different real numbers stay different, and adding or multiplying two real numbers gives the same answer in 
C as in 
R. The Real Numbers inside the Complex Numbers Let \iota \colon 
R 	o 
C be the map \iota(a) \coloneqq (a, 0). Then \iota is injective (@fd2:def-injective), and for all a, c \in 
R, \iota(a + c) = \iota(a) + \iota(c) , \qquad \iota(ac) = \iota(a)\, \iota(c) , \qquad \iota(1) = (1, 0) . Moreover (a, b) = \iota(a) + \iota(b)\, i for all a, b \in 
R, and i \cdot i = \iota(-1). Each claim is one application of the definitions: write both sides as pairs and compare coordinates. The facts about 
R needed are that 0 is neutral for addition (so subtracting 0 changes nothing), that 1 is neutral for multiplication, and that a product with 0 is 0, which kills the extra terms of the multiplication formula. Let a, c \in 
R. If \iota(a) = \iota(c), then (a, 0) = (c, 0), so a = c by @fd2:def-ordered-pair; hence \iota is injective. By @def-complex-numbers, \iota(a) + \iota(c) = (a + c, \; 0 + 0) = (a + c, \; 0) = \iota(a + c) , and, since a \cdot 0 = 0 \cdot c = 0 \cdot 0 = 0 in 
R (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), \iota(a)\, \iota(c) = (ac - 0 \cdot 0, \; a \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot c) = (ac, \; 0) = \iota(ac) . The equation \iota(1) = (1, 0) is the definition of \iota. Next, for a, b \in 
R, \iota(b)\, i = (b, 0)(0, 1) = (b \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1, \; b \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0) = (0, b) , so \iota(a) + \iota(b)\, i = (a, 0) + (0, b) = (a, b). Finally i \cdot i = (-1, 0) = \iota(-1) by the computation before the proposition. Identification. From now on we write a for \iota(a) and regard 
R as a subset of 
C. In particular 0 = (0, 0) and 1 = (1, 0). This is a convenient abuse of notation made honest by the injective embedding, exactly as Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.2 wrote n for the integer \iota(n): because \iota is injective, different real numbers stay different, and because it preserves + and \cdot, a sum or product of real numbers is the same whether computed in 
R or in 
C. With this convention the proposition reads (a, b) = a + bi \quad 	ext{for all } a, b \in 
R , \qquad i^2 = i \cdot i = -1 . So the notation a + bi is honest: it is a computation with the definitions, not a new symbol. Comparing real and imaginary parts now reads: for a, b, c, d \in 
R, a + bi = c + di \iff a = c 	ext{ and } b = d . For z = a + bi with a, b \in 
R we have \operatorname{Re} z = a and \operatorname{Im} z = b. A real number a = a + 0i is a complex number whose imaginary part is 0, and 0 = 0 + 0i is the only complex number with both parts 0. The point i = 0 + 1i has real part 0 and imaginary part 1. The rule “a + bi = c + di gives a = c and b = d” needs a, b, c, d to be real. Without that it fails: 0 + 1 \cdot i = i + 0 \cdot i, yet 0 
e i. Before comparing parts, write each side as a + bi with a and b known to be real. [First Computations in 
C] Compute (2 + 3i)(1 - i), the products i \cdot i, (i \cdot i) \cdot i and  igl((i \cdot i) \cdot i igr) \cdot i, and the product (a + bi)(a - bi) for real a, b. Here 1 - i is 1 + (-1)i. By the multiplication rule with a = 2, b = 3, c = 1, d = -1, (2 + 3i)(1 - i) =  igl(2 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot (-1) igr) +  igl(2 \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot 1 igr) i = 5 + i . We already know i \cdot i = -1 = (-1, 0). Then (i \cdot i) \cdot i = (-1, 0)(0, 1) = (0 - 0, \; -1 + 0) = (0, -1) = -i , writing -i for 0 + (-1)i, and  igl((i \cdot i) \cdot i igr) \cdot i = (0, -1)(0, 1) =  igl(0 - (-1), \; 0 + 0 igr) = (1, 0) = 1 . Finally, with a - bi = a + (-b)i, (a + bi)(a - bi) =  igl(a^2 - b(-b) igr) +  igl(a(-b) + ba igr) i = a^2 + b^2 , where a^2 = aa and b^2 = bb are computed in 
R. This product is a real number, and it is non-negative, since a^2 \ge 0 and b^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) for a non-zero real, and 0^2 = 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so a^2 + b^2 \ge 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). We meet it again in Section 1.2, as the square of the length of a + bi. The last product is the first hint of how division will work: multiplying a + bi by a - bi lands in the real numbers, where division is familiar. Compute (1 + i)(1 + i). Is \operatorname{Im}(3 - 4i) equal to -4i? By the multiplication rule, (1 + i)(1 + i) = (1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 1) + (1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1)i = 2i. No: 3 - 4i = 3 + (-4)i with 3, -4 \in 
R, so \operatorname{Im}(3 - 4i) = -4, a real number. The number -4i is not real, since its imaginary part is -4 
e 0. A non-example by minimal change. Change one sign in the multiplication rule: define (a, b) * (c, d) \coloneqq (ac + bd, \; ad + bc) , which is what expanding gives if we pretend j^2 = +1 instead. Addition is unchanged. This product is still commutative, by commutativity in 
R, and (1, 0) is still an identity element: (a, b) * (1, 0) = (a + 0, \; 0 + b) = (a, b). But (1, 1) * (1, -1) =  igl(1 - 1, \; -1 + 1 igr) = (0, 0) , so two non-zero elements multiply to zero. Division breaks down too: (1, 1) * (c, d) = (c + d, \; d + c) can never equal the identity element (1, 0), because that would need c + d = 1 and d + c = 0 at once. So the non-zero element (1, 1) has no inverse. The single sign in ac - bd is what makes division possible, as Section 1.2 will show. Exercise B3 finds every element that goes wrong in this way. Why this definition. We could have tried to postulate a number i with i^2 = -1, but a postulate is only as safe as the consistency of what it asserts. Pairs of reals are sets we already have, so 
C exists as soon as 
R does, and every law we want must now be proved. The multiplication formula is not a free choice either: Exercise C1 shows that in any field K containing 
R, whose sum and product agree with those of 
R on real numbers, and containing a square root j of -1, the product of a + bj and c + dj is forced to be (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)j. The minimal change above shows that a different formula really does give a different, and worse, system. The laws of arithmetic Before computing freely, we should confirm that rearranging, regrouping and expanding brackets are legal in 
C. The definition does not promise this; it has to be checked. [Arithmetic Laws in 
C] For all z, w, u \in 
C: 1. z + w = w + z and zw = wz; 2. (z + w) + u = z + (w + u) and (zw)u = z(wu); 3. z(w + u) = zw + zu; 4. z + 0 = z, z \cdot 1 = z, and z + (-z) = 0, where -(a + bi) \coloneqq (-a) + (-b)i for a, b \in 
R. Every law reduces to the corresponding law for real numbers once both sides are written as pairs and compared part by part. Addition is coordinate by coordinate, so its laws are immediate. For multiplication the only real work is associativity: expand both sides and see that they produce the same four terms in each coordinate. Let z = a + bi, w = c + di and u = e + fi with a, b, c, d, e, f \in 
R. In each part we compute both sides with @def-complex-numbers and compare real and imaginary parts, using the field laws of 
R (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) and the algebra of @fd3:prp-ring-algebra. Since addition acts coordinate by coordinate, the laws for addition in (a), (b) and (d) are the same laws in 
R, applied to each coordinate; for (d), z + 0 = (a + 0) + (b + 0)i = z and z + (-z) = (a + (-a)) + (b + (-b))i = 0. (a) By definition zw = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i and wz = (ca - db) + (cb + da)i. These are equal because real multiplication and addition are commutative. (b) Expanding with the definition twice gives  egin{aligned} (zw)u &=  igl((ac - bd)e - (ad + bc)f igr) \ &\qquad +  igl((ac - bd)f + (ad + bc)e igr)i \end{aligned} and  egin{aligned} z(wu) &=  igl(a(ce - df) - b(cf + de) igr) \ &\qquad +  igl(a(cf + de) + b(ce - df) igr)i . \end{aligned} Multiplying out with the distributive law of 
R, both real parts equal ace - adf - bcf - bde, and both imaginary parts equal acf + ade + bce - bdf. Hence (zw)u = z(wu). (c) We have w + u = (c + e) + (d + f)i, so  egin{aligned} z(w + u) &=  igl(a(c + e) - b(d + f) igr) +  igl(a(d + f) + b(c + e) igr)i \ &=  igl((ac - bd) + (ae - bf) igr) +  igl((ad + bc) + (af + be) igr)i , \end{aligned} which is zw + zu by the definitions of the product and the sum. (d) With 1 = 1 + 0i, we get z \cdot 1 = (a \cdot 1 - b \cdot 0) + (a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 1)i = a + bi = z. The equations for addition were shown above. This proves the proposition. C, with the operations of @def-complex-numbers, is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0. Every result proved for commutative rings therefore holds in 
C without a new proof. From @fd3:prp-ring-algebra: 0, 1 and negatives are unique, -(-z) = z, z \cdot 0 = 0, (-z)w = -(zw), (-z)(-w) = zw, and (z + w)^2 = z^2 + 2zw + w^2, where z^2 \coloneqq zz. The remaining field axiom (F8), inverses of non-zero elements, is the subject of Section 1.2. From now on we compute in 
C exactly as in 
R: expand brackets, collect terms, and replace i^2 by -1. The proposition is what makes that habit legitimate. For instance, (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 - abi + abi - b^2 i^2 = a^2 + b^2 agrees with @exm-complex-arithmetic. Powers and a factorization Powers in 
C are defined exactly as powers in an ordered field were, and that definition never used the order. We state it, and the laws of powers, for an arbitrary commutative ring, because the same proofs serve every commutative ring and later chapters need them in that generality. Powers. Let R be a commutative ring and z \in R. The powers z^n, for n \in 
N, are given by @fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b), with X = R, starting value 1 and step (k, y) \mapsto yz: z^0 \coloneqq 1 , \qquad z^{n+1} \coloneqq z^n z \quad 	ext{for every } n \in 
N . This is the recursion of Sets and Functions, Section 3.3 (@fd2:def-power), stated there for real numbers, and the same recursion as @fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). In particular z^1 = 1 \cdot z = z and z^2 = z^1 z = zz, matching the z^2 of @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d). [Laws of Powers in a Commutative Ring] Let R be a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), let z, w \in R, and let m, n \in 
N. 1. z^{m+n} = z^m z^n. 2. (z^m)^n = z^{mn}. 3. (zw)^n = z^n w^n. 4. If R is a field and z 
e 0, then z^n 
e 0. The definition of z^n is a recursion on n, so every law is proved by induction on n, peeling off the last factor with z^{n+1} = z^n z. Each inductive step rests on one ingredient: associativity (F5) for (a), the law (a) for (b), associativity and commutativity (F5), (F6) for (c), and the absence of zero divisors in a field for (d). Each part is proved by @fd1:ax-induction (through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) on n, with z, w and m fixed. (a) For n = 0: z^{m+0} = z^m = z^m \cdot 1 = z^m z^0, by (F7). If z^{m+n} = z^m z^n, then z^{m+(n+1)} = z^{(m+n)+1} = z^{m+n} z = (z^m z^n) z = z^m (z^n z) = z^m z^{n+1} , by the recursion, the hypothesis and associativity (F5). (b) For n = 0: (z^m)^0 = 1 = z^0 = z^{m \cdot 0}. If (z^m)^n = z^{mn}, then (z^m)^{n+1} = (z^m)^n z^m = z^{mn} z^m = z^{mn + m} = z^{m(n+1)}, by the recursion, the hypothesis and (a). (c) For n = 0: (zw)^0 = 1 = 1 \cdot 1 = z^0 w^0. If (zw)^n = z^n w^n, then (zw)^{n+1} = (zw)^n (zw) = (z^n w^n)(zw) = (z^n z)(w^n w) = z^{n+1} w^{n+1} , where the third equality regroups and reorders the four factors by (F5) and (F6). (d) Let R be a field and z 
e 0. For n = 0: z^0 = 1 
e 0, by the definition of a field. If z^n 
e 0, then z^{n+1} = z^n z is a product of two non-zero elements, so it is non-zero, since a field has no zero divisors (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)). Parts (a)–(c) are the laws of Sets and Functions, Section 3.3 (@fd2:prp-power-laws (a)–(c)), proved there for real numbers; on 
N = \omega, which is not a ring, law (a) is @fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity (a), proved by the same induction. The proofs above are the same inductions, and they use only the ring axioms. For a real number a, the power a^n is the same whether computed in 
R or in 
C. Indeed \iota(a^0) = \iota(1) = 1, and if \iota(a^n) = \iota(a)^n, then \iota(a^{n+1}) = \iota(a^n a) = \iota(a^n)\,\iota(a) = \iota(a)^{n+1}, by @prp-reals-embed-complex; induction (@fd1:ax-induction) does the rest. So the identification of 
R with a subset of 
C is safe for powers too. In the notation of powers, @exm-complex-arithmetic computed i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i and i^4 = 1; by (a), (b), every multiple of 4 gives i^{4q} = (i^4)^q = 1^q = 1, since 1^{q+1} = 1^q \cdot 1 and induction give 1^q = 1. Exercise B1 turns this into a rule for every power of i. Compute i^{10} and (1 + i)^4, citing the parts of @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring you use. By (a) and (b), i^{10} = i^{8} i^{2} = (i^4)^2 i^2 = 1^2 \cdot (-1) = -1. By (b), (1 + i)^4 =  igl((1 + i)^2 igr)^2 = (2i)^2, and by (c), (2i)^2 = 2^2 i^2 = 4 \cdot (-1) = -4, using (1 + i)^2 = 2i from the first Quick check. Finite sums. One identity about powers is used repeatedly in this chapter and later, and it needs sums of several terms. For elements a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots of a commutative ring R and n \in 
N, the sum \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k is defined by the recursion of @fd2:def-sum-product, with R as the set of values and the index starting at 0: the empty sum \sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k is 0, and \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k + a_n \quad 	ext{for every } n \in 
N . So the recursion appends the last term. We also write a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_n for this sum. Multiplying a sum by c \in R multiplies each term:  igl(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k igr) c = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k c, by induction on n, since 0 \cdot c = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)) and the step is one use of the distributive law (F9). [Difference of Powers] Let R be a commutative ring, let z, w \in R, and let n \in 
N with n \ge 1. Then z^n - w^n = (z - w) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z^k w^{n-1-k} . In particular z^n - 1 = (z - 1)(1 + z + z^2 + \dots + z^{n-1}). For n = 2 this is z^2 - w^2 = (z - w)(w + z), and for n = 3 it is z^3 - w^3 = (z - w)(w^2 + zw + z^2). To pass from n to n + 1, split z^{n+1} - w^{n+1} so that the case n appears: z^{n+1} - w^{n+1} = (z^n - w^n)w + z^n(z - w). The first piece is (z - w) times the old sum times w, and the second supplies the one new term z^n, which the recursion appends at the end. For n \ge 1 write S_n \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z^k w^{n-1-k}. We prove z^{m+1} - w^{m+1} = (z - w) S_{m+1} for every m \in 
N, by @fd1:ax-induction (through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) on m. For m = 0: S_1 = z^0 w^0 = 1, so (z - w) S_1 = z - w = z^1 - w^1. Let n \coloneqq m + 1 \ge 1 and suppose z^n - w^n = (z - w) S_n. Expanding with (F9) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c), (z^n - w^n) w + z^n (z - w) = z^n w - w^n w + z^n z - z^n w = z^{n+1} - w^{n+1} , by the recursion for powers. By the hypothesis and the rule for multiplying a sum by w, (z^n - w^n) w = (z - w) S_n w = (z - w) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z^k w^{n-k} , since w^{n-1-k} w = w^{n-k} for k \le n - 1 (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a)). Since z^n = z^n w^0, the recursion for sums gives  egin{aligned} z^{n+1} - w^{n+1} &= (z - w) \Bigl( \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z^k w^{n-k} + z^n w^0 \Bigr) \ &= (z - w) \sum_{k=0}^{n} z^k w^{n-k} = (z - w) S_{n+1} . \end{aligned} This completes the induction. The particular case is w = 1, since 1^j = 1 for every j \in 
N. The lemma is the algebra behind the formula for a finite geometric sum: if z - 1 has an inverse, then 1 + z + \dots + z^{n-1} = (z^n - 1)(z - 1)^{-1}. Section 1.6 uses it again, for real numbers, to show that 0 \le s < t gives s^n < t^n. Here we need only the identity. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Compute (2 - i)(3 + 4i), and the real and imaginary parts of i(1 + i). 2. True or false, with a reason: the equation (a, b) = a + bi, for a, b \in 
R, needs a proof. 3. Which laws in @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws need a genuine computation, and which follow coordinate by coordinate from the same laws in 
R? 4. True or false, with a reason: if z \in 
C and z^2 = 0, then z = 0. Prove it by comparing real and imaginary parts, without using that 
C is a field. (a) (2 - i)(3 + 4i) = 6 + 8i - 3i - 4i^2 = 6 + 4 + 5i = 10 + 5i. And i(1 + i) = i + i^2 = -1 + i, so \operatorname{Re} igl(i(1 + i) igr) = -1 and \operatorname{Im} igl(i(1 + i) igr) = 1. (b) True. The symbols a, b and i denote the pairs (a, 0), (b, 0), (0, 1), and a + bi is a sum and a product of pairs. That it equals (a, b) is a computation with @def-complex-numbers; it is part of @prp-reals-embed-complex. (c) The laws for addition, in (a), (b) and (d), hold coordinate by coordinate. Commutativity of multiplication, distributivity and z \cdot 1 = z are one-line computations. Associativity of multiplication is the one law that needs a genuine expansion: both sides have four terms in each part, and they agree only after multiplying out. (d) True. Let z = a + bi. Then z^2 = (a^2 - b^2) + 2abi, so z^2 = 0 gives a^2 - b^2 = 0 and 2ab = 0, by comparing parts. Since 2 
e 0 in 
R and 
R has no zero divisors (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)), a = 0 or b = 0. If a = 0, then -b^2 = 0, so b^2 = 0 and b = 0 by the same rule; if b = 0, then a^2 = 0 and a = 0. So z = 0. (Once Section 1.2 has shown that 
C is a field, this follows at once from @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d) in 
C.) B. Practice [B1: Powers of i] Let n \in 
N, and let r be the remainder of n on division by 4. Prove that i^n = i^r. Hence compute i^{2026}. By division with remainder (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, with n \in 
N \subseteq 
Z and divisor 4) there are integers q, r with n = 4q + r and 0 \le r < 4. Also q \ge 0: if q \le -1, then n \le -4 + r < 0, which is false. So q, r \in 
N. By @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a) and (b), and i^4 = 1 (@exm-complex-arithmetic), i^n = i^{4q} i^r = (i^4)^q i^r = 1^q i^r = i^r , where 1^q = 1 by induction on q (1^{q+1} = 1^q \cdot 1). So i^n is 1, i, -1, -i according as r = 0, 1, 2, 3. Hence, since 2026 = 4 \cdot 506 + 2, i^{2026} = i^2 = -1. [B2] 1. Use @lem-difference-of-powers to factor z^3 - 1 and z^4 - 1 in 
C, and check the second factorization at z = i. 2. Verify (1 + i)^4 = -4 using (1 + i)^2 = 2i and @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring. Hence show that, for every z \in 
C, z^4 + 4 =  igl(z - (1 + i) igr) igl(z^3 + (1 + i) z^2 + 2i z + (-2 + 2i) igr) . (a) With n = 3 and n = 4, z^3 - 1 = (z - 1)(1 + z + z^2) , \qquad z^4 - 1 = (z - 1)(1 + z + z^2 + z^3) . At z = i: the left side is i^4 - 1 = 0, and on the right 1 + i + i^2 + i^3 = 1 + i - 1 - i = 0, so both sides are 0. (b) By (b) of the proposition with m = n = 2, and then (c), (1 + i)^4 =  igl((1 + i)^2 igr)^2 = (2i)^2 = 2^2 i^2 = -4 . Let w \coloneqq 1 + i. Then w^2 = 2i and w^3 = w^2 w = 2i(1 + i) = -2 + 2i. By @lem-difference-of-powers with n = 4, whose sum is w^3 + z w^2 + z^2 w + z^3, z^4 - w^4 = (z - w) igl(z^3 + w z^2 + w^2 z + w^3 igr) . Since w^4 = -4, the left side is z^4 + 4, and substituting w, w^2, w^3 gives the displayed factorization. In particular 1 + i is a root of z^4 + 4. [B3: The zero divisors of the minimal change] Let * be the product (a, b) * (c, d) \coloneqq (ac + bd, \; ad + bc) on 
R^2 of the non-example in this section. Call a non-zero p \in

e b^2, then a^2 - b^2 
e 0 has an inverse in 
R, and t \coloneqq (a^2 - b^2)^{-1} gives (1, 0). (\Leftarrow) Let (a, b)

R). If b = a, then (a, a) * (1, -1) = (a - a, \; -a + a) = (0, 0); if b = -a, then (a, -a) * (1, 1) = (a - a, \; a - a) = (0, 0). In both cases the second factor is non-zero, so (a, b) is a zero divisor. Such an element also has no inverse: (a, a) * (c, d) =  igl(a(c + d), \; a(c + d) igr) has equal coordinates and (a, -a) * (c, d) =  igl(a(c - d), \; -a(c - d) igr) has opposite coordinates, while (1, 0) has neither, since 1 
e 0 and 1 
e -0 = 0. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive). Let a^2 
e b^2, and suppose (a, b) * (c, d) = (0, 0), that is, ac + bd = 0 and ad + bc = 0. Multiply the first equation by a and the second by b, and subtract: a^2 c + abd - abd - b^2 c = 0, that is, (a^2 - b^2) c = 0. Multiply the first by b and the second by a, and subtract: (b^2 - a^2) d = 0. Since a^2 - b^2 
e 0 and 
R has no zero divisors, c = 0 and d = 0. So the only q with (a, b) * q = (0, 0) is q = (0, 0), and (a, b) is not a zero divisor. No associativity of * was needed. For example, (1, 1) is a zero divisor, as in the text, and (2, 1) is not: (2, 1) * (2/3, -1/3) = (4/3 - 1/3, \; -2/3 + 2/3) = (1, 0). C. Going deeper [C1: There is only one way to adjoin a square root of minus one] Let K be a field (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) with 
R \subseteq K, such that the sum and the product of K, applied to two real numbers, are their sum and product in

title: 1.2 Conjugate, Modulus, and Division
content:
Conjugate, Modulus, and Division Section 1.1 built 
C and showed that it is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 (@prp-complex-arithmetic-laws). One field axiom is still missing: (F8), which asks for an inverse of every non-zero element. To divide by 3 + 4i, we want a number to multiply by that lands in the real numbers, where division is familiar. The product (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2 of @exm-complex-arithmetic shows which number does the job. This section gives its two ingredients names, the conjugate and the modulus, proves the rules they obey, and concludes that 
C is a field. Conjugate and modulus A complex number z = a + bi is a point (a, b) of the plane. Two pieces of plane geometry turn out to be algebra in disguise: the mirror image of z in the horizontal axis, and the distance of z from 0. The mirror image changes the sign of b. The distance, by Pythagoras, is the square root of a^2 + b^2, the very number that appeared in @exm-complex-arithmetic. Square roots of non-negative real numbers exist and are unique in every complete ordered field (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), so we may use them in 
R: for x \in 
R with x \ge 0, \sqrt{x} is the unique y \in 
R with y \ge 0 and y^2 = x. Conjugating reflects a point in the real axis; the modulus is its distance from the origin. Conjugate and Modulus Let z = a + bi \in 
C with a, b \in 
R. The complex conjugate of z is \conj{z} \coloneqq a - bi . The modulus (or absolute value) of z is the real number \abs{z} \coloneqq \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} , the non-negative square root of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots in 
R. In words: the conjugate keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part, \operatorname{Re} \conj{z} = \operatorname{Re} z and \operatorname{Im} \conj{z} = -\operatorname{Im} z. The modulus is a real number, never negative, and its square is a^2 + b^2 = (\operatorname{Re} z)^2 + (\operatorname{Im} z)^2. Well-definedness. Since z determines a and b (compare real and imaginary parts, Section 1.1), the right-hand sides depend only on z. The square root exists because its argument is non-negative: a^2 \ge 0 and b^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), with 0^2 = 0 when the number is 0), so a^2 + b^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). And 
R is complete (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), which is the hypothesis of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. This is where the completeness of 
R enters the chapter. Over 
Q alone the definition would break down at once: \abs{1 + i} would have to be a rational number whose square is 2, and there is none (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two). Examples. A point with integer distance. For z = 3 + 4i: \conj{z} = 3 - 4i, and \abs{z} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5. The last step is the uniqueness clause of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots: 5 \ge 0 and 5^2 = 25, so 5 is the non-negative square root of 25. The unit i. \conj{i} = \conj{0 + 1i} = 0 - 1i = -i, and \abs{i} = \sqrt{0 + 1} = 1, since 1 \ge 0 and 1^2 = 1. The degenerate case z = 0. \conj{0} = 0 and \abs{0} = \sqrt{0} = 0. We show below that 0 is the only complex number with modulus 0; that one fact is what makes division possible. A real number. For a \in 
R, \conj{a} = a and \abs{a} = \sqrt{a^2}. The symbol \abs{a} already had a meaning for real a: the absolute value of an ordered field (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field). The next proposition shows the two meanings agree, so the notation does not clash. [The Modulus Extends the Absolute Value] Let a \in 
R \subseteq 
C. Then \conj{a} = a, and the modulus \sqrt{a^2 + 0^2} of a equals the absolute value of a in the ordered field 
R (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field). Write a = a + 0i. Then \conj{a} = a - 0i = a, since 0 \cdot i = i \cdot 0 = 0 by (F6) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), and -0 = 0 because 0 + 0 = 0 and negatives are unique (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)), all in the commutative ring 
C. The modulus of a is \sqrt{a^2 + 0^2} = \sqrt{a^2}, the unique non-negative real number whose square is a^2. The absolute value \abs{a} of the ordered field 
R is non-negative and satisfies \abs{a}^2 = a^2 (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), (b)). By the uniqueness clause of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots, the two are equal. So the modulus extends the absolute value: on 
R \subseteq 
C it is the old \abs{\cdot}, and every result about \abs{x} for real x stays true with the new reading. For instance \abs{-3} = 3, whichever definition we use. The Triangle Inequality The modulus of Section 1.2 measures a complex number by a real one. Picture z = a + bi as the point (a, b) of the plane: by Pythagoras, \abs{z} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} is its distance from the origin, and \abs{z - w} is the distance between the points z and w. In a triangle, one side is never longer than the other two together. This section proves the algebraic form of that fact, \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w}, from the definitions alone. The picture motivates it; no step of the proof uses it. Why the old proof does not transfer For an ordered field, Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 proved \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} by trapping (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)). Each of x and y lies between \pm its absolute value, -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x} (part (c) there); adding the two traps traps x + y between \pm(\abs{x} + \abs{y}), and part (d) reads that as the inequality. That route needs x \le \abs{x}: a comparison between x itself and a number. For a complex z, “z \le \abs{z}” compares a complex number with a real one, and 
C has been given no order in which to make the comparison. Section 1.4 shows that no order compatible with the arithmetic of 
C exists (@prp-complex-not-orderable). So the proof must compare real numbers only. Two kinds of real number are at hand. Moduli are real, and so are real parts. The device that connects them to the arithmetic of 
C is the identity \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u} of @thm-conjugate-properties (c). A modulus is a square root, and square roots do not add well; its square is a product, and products expand. So we will compare squares and then come back. Comparing squares. Coming back from squares to the numbers needs one rule about the real numbers. Let p, q \in 
R with p \ge 0 and q \ge 0. Then p \le q \iff p^2 \le q^2 , \qquad\qquad p = q \iff p^2 = q^2 , and likewise with < on both sides. The strict form is @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g). For the first equivalence: if p < q, then p^2 < q^2 by (g), and if p = q the squares agree. Conversely, if p^2 \le q^2 and yet q < p, then (g) gives q^2 < p^2, which contradicts p^2 \le q^2 by trichotomy (O1); so p \le q. The second equivalence follows from the first, applied in both directions, and trichotomy. In words: for non-negative reals, squaring neither creates nor destroys a comparison. Both hypotheses p \ge 0 and q \ge 0 matter: (-2)^2 > 1^2, and yet -2 < 1. The real part is at most the modulus The single estimate the proof needs is that a real part never exceeds the modulus. Fatal errors (0 for the step): expanding \abs{z - w}^2 as (z - w)^2; comparing z\conj{w} with a real number.

title: 1.4 Square Roots, Quadratic Equations, and the Missing Order
content:
Square Roots, Quadratic Equations, and the Missing Order Logic and Proof, Section 7.1 needed, in one of its checks, the fact that every complex number has a complex square root, and took it there as a school fact about polar form. This section proves it, with no angles at all: a square root of a complex number is built from two square roots of non-negative reals, which Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 6 provides (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). The quadratic formula follows, for complex coefficients. Then we see what 
C has lost on the way from 
R: it has no order compatible with its arithmetic, and the rule \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{xy} has no complex version. Square roots from real square roots The question is: given z = a + bi, find w = x + yi with w^2 = z. Since w^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + 2xyi, comparing real and imaginary parts turns the question into two real equations, x^2 - y^2 = a , \qquad 2xy = b . The answer is an explicit formula in a, b and \abs{z}. [Square Roots of Complex Numbers] Let z = a + bi \in 
C with a, b \in 
R and z 
e 0, and let r \coloneqq \abs{z}. Put s \coloneqq 1 if b \ge 0 and s \coloneqq -1 if b < 0, and x \coloneqq \sqrt{ rac{r + a}{2}} , \qquad y \coloneqq s \sqrt{ rac{r - a}{2}} , \qquad w \coloneqq x + yi . Then: 1. w^2 = z; 2. for u \in 
C, u^2 = z if and only if u = w or u = -w; 3. w 
e -w. For z = 0: u^2 = 0 if and only if u = 0. In words: every non-zero complex number has exactly two square roots, w and -w, and the formula finds one of them; 0 has exactly one. Try it first (ten minutes): find w with w^2 = 3 + 4i by writing w = x + yi. What do you do with the two equations you get? For 3 + 4i the two equations are x^2 - y^2 = 3 and 2xy = 4. The natural attempt eliminates y = 2/x and arrives at x^4 - 3x^2 - 4 = 0, a quartic; it can be solved, but it hides what is going on, and in general it needs the quadratic formula before we have it. The missing piece is a third equation, and it comes from the modulus. If w^2 = z, then \abs{w}^2 = \abs{w^2} = \abs{z} by @thm-conjugate-properties (d), that is, x^2 + y^2 = r. Now the first equation and the third give x^2 and y^2 by adding and subtracting: x^2 = (r + a)/2, y^2 = (r - a)/2. That fixes x and y up to sign, and the second equation 2xy = b says which signs go together: xy has the sign of b. For 3 + 4i: r = 5, x^2 = 4, y^2 = 1, xy > 0, so w = \pm(2 + i). The proof runs this forward: define x and y by the formulas, check w^2 = z, and get “only \pm w” from the field axioms. Before reading on: why does the sign of b decide whether x and y have the same sign? The proof uses one small rule about real square roots: for p, q \in 
R with p, q \ge 0, \sqrt{p}\,\sqrt{q} = \sqrt{pq} . Both sides are non-negative (a product of non-negative reals is non-negative), and the square of the left side is (\sqrt p)^2 (\sqrt q)^2 = pq, by commutativity; so the left side is the non-negative number whose square is pq, which is the right side by the uniqueness in @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. The rule is about non-negative reals only; the last part of this section shows that it has no complex version. The roots exist. By @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus, \abs{a} = \abs{\operatorname{Re} z} \le r, so -r \le a \le r (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). Hence r + a \ge 0 and r - a \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), (b)). Halving keeps this: for p \ge 0, either p > 0 and then p/2 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (b), with \varepsilon = p), or p = 0 and then p/2 = 0 \cdot (1/2) = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). So (r + a)/2 \ge 0 and (r - a)/2 \ge 0. So the two square roots in the definition of x and y exist (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). (a) Since s^2 = 1, x^2 - y^2 =  rac{r + a}{2} - s^2 \,  rac{r - a}{2} =  rac{r + a}{2} -  rac{r - a}{2} = a . For the imaginary part, the rule for real square roots gives  egin{aligned} 2xy &= 2s\sqrt{ rac{r + a}{2}}\sqrt{ rac{r - a}{2}} = 2s\sqrt{ rac{r^2 - a^2}{4}} \ &= s\sqrt{r^2 - a^2} = s\sqrt{b^2} = s\abs{b} = b . \end{aligned} Here the third equality is 2\sqrt{t/4} = \sqrt{4}\sqrt{t/4} = \sqrt{t}, by the same rule and \sqrt 4 = 2; the fourth uses r^2 = a^2 + b^2 (@def-conjugate-modulus); the fifth holds because \abs{b} \ge 0 and \abs{b}^2 = b^2 (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), (b)), with uniqueness in @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots; and the last because s\abs{b} = b by the definitions of s and of \abs{b} (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field), in each of the two cases b \ge 0 and b < 0. Hence w^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + 2xyi = a + bi = z, by the multiplication rule of @def-complex-numbers. (b) Let u \in 
C. Since 
C is a commutative ring, (u - w)(u + w) = u^2 - w^2 (@prp-complex-arithmetic-laws, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). If u^2 = z, then u^2 - w^2 = z - z = 0 by (a), so (u - w)(u + w) = 0. Since 
C is a field (@thm-complex-numbers-field), it has no zero divisors (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)), so u - w = 0 or u + w = 0, that is, u = w or u = -w. Conversely w^2 = z by (a), and (-w)^2 = w^2 = z by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c). (c) First w 
e 0, since w^2 = z 
e 0 and 0^2 = 0. Suppose w = -w. Then 2w = w + w = 0. But 2 = 1 + 1 
e 0 in 
C: it is the real number 2, which is positive in 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)), and 
R \subseteq 
C by the injective embedding of @prp-reals-embed-complex. So 2w = 0 with 2 
e 0 and w 
e 0 contradicts the absence of zero divisors. Hence w 
e -w. Finally, for z = 0: 0^2 = 0, and if u^2 = u \cdot u = 0, then u = 0 by @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d). This proves the proposition. The answer to the prompt: x is non-negative by construction, and y is s times a non-negative number, so xy is s times a non-negative number, and 2xy must equal b. If b > 0, then x and y must both be non-zero with the same sign; if b < 0, opposite signs. When b = 0 the choice of s does not matter, because then one of x, y is 0. The proposition proves what Logic and Proof, Section 7.1 assumed, and it is stronger: it counts the roots. It uses only the field 
C, its modulus, and square roots of non-negative reals; no angle, cosine or sine appears. That matters later: Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 5 proves the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra using square roots in exactly this form. [Square Roots of 5 - 12i] Find all w \in 
C with w^2 = 5 - 12i. Write w = x + yi with x, y \in 
R. Comparing real and imaginary parts in (x^2 - y^2) + 2xyi = 5 - 12i gives x^2 - y^2 = 5 \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad xy = -6 . Taking moduli, by @thm-conjugate-properties (d), x^2 + y^2 = \abs{w}^2 = \abs{5 - 12i} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13. Adding and subtracting, x^2 = 9 and y^2 = 4, so x = \pm 3 and y = \pm 2. Since xy = -6 < 0, x and y have opposite signs. Hence w = 3 - 2i or w = -3 + 2i. Check: (3 - 2i)^2 = 9 - 12i + 4i^2 = 5 - 12i, and (-3 + 2i)^2 = (3 - 2i)^2. The formula of @prp-complex-square-roots gives the same root: a = 5, b = -12 < 0, so s = -1; r = 13, x = \sqrt{18/2} = 3 and y = -\sqrt{8/2} = -2. By part (b) there are no other roots. Find the square roots of -4 and of 2i. For -4: a = -4, b = 0, r = 4, so x = \sqrt{0} = 0 and y = \sqrt{8/2} = 2; the roots are \pm 2i, and indeed (2i)^2 = -4. For 2i: a = 0, b = 2, r = 2, so x = \sqrt{1} = 1 and y = 1; the roots are \pm(1 + i), and (1 + i)^2 = 1 + 2i - 1 = 2i. The quadratic formula With square roots in hand, a quadratic equation with complex coefficients is solved exactly as in school: complete the square. The only difference is that we never need to ask whether the discriminant is negative. [Quadratic Formula over the Complex Numbers] Let a, b, c \in 
C with a 
e 0, and let d \in 
C be a square root of b^2 - 4ac (one exists by @prp-complex-square-roots). Then for z \in 
C, az^2 + bz + c = 0 \iff z =  rac{-b + d}{2a} \ 	ext{ or } \ z =  rac{-b - d}{2a} . The two solutions coincide if and only if b^2 - 4ac = 0. Here a, b, c are complex numbers, in a departure from the chapter’s habit of reserving these letters for reals; the statement is the school formula, and keeps its letters. The choice of d does not matter: the other square root is -d (@prp-complex-square-roots (b)), which swaps the two solutions. Complete the square, as in school: after multiplying by 4a, the equation says that 2az + b is a square root of b^2 - 4ac. The square roots of b^2 - 4ac are exactly d and -d, and solving the two linear equations 2az + b = \pm d gives the formula. Multiply by 4a and complete the square. By the ring laws (@prp-complex-arithmetic-laws) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d), 4a(az^2 + bz + c) = 4a^2z^2 + 4abz + 4ac = (2az + b)^2 - (b^2 - 4ac) . Now 4a 
e 0, since 4 
e 0 in 
C (as for 2 in the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots (c)) and a 
e 0, and 
C has no zero divisors (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)). So az^2 + bz + c = 0 if and only if (2az + b)^2 = d^2, that is, (2az + b - d)(2az + b + d) = 0, as in the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots (b). By the absence of zero divisors again, this holds if and only if 2az + b = d or 2az + b = -d. Since 2a 
e 0, these say z = (-b + d)/(2a) or z = (-b - d)/(2a). The two solutions coincide if and only if d = -d, that is, 2d = 0, that is, d = 0 (as 2 
e 0). And d = 0 if and only if d^2 = 0 (no zero divisors), that is, b^2 - 4ac = 0. This proves the corollary. Example. Solve z^2 - (3 + i)z + (2 + 2i) = 0. Here a = 1, and the discriminant is (3 + i)^2 - 4(2 + 2i) = (8 + 6i) - (8 + 8i) = -2i . The formula of @prp-complex-square-roots, applied to -2i (real part 0, imaginary part -2 < 0, modulus 2), gives x = \sqrt{2/2} = 1 and y = -\sqrt{2/2} = -1, so d = 1 - i; indeed (1 - i)^2 = 1 - 2i - 1 = -2i. The solutions are z =  rac{(3 + i) + (1 - i)}{2} = 2 \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad z =  rac{(3 + i) - (1 - i)}{2} = 1 + i . Check: their sum is 3 + i and their product is 2 + 2i, the negative of the middle coefficient and the constant term, as they should be for (z - 2)(z - (1 + i)). No order on the complex numbers In 
R, and in every ordered field, a non-zero square is positive (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). In 
C, i is non-zero and its square is -1. If 
C carried an order of the kind 
R has, -1 would have to be positive, and so would 1. That is already the proof. [The Complex Numbers Cannot Be Ordered] There is no relation < on 
C with which (
C, +, \cdot, <) is an ordered field in the sense of @fd3:def-ordered-ring-and-field. Suppose < is a relation on 
C with which 
C is an ordered field. Since i = (0, 1) 
e (0, 0) = 0, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) gives i^2 > 0, that is, -1 > 0 (@prp-reals-embed-complex: i \cdot i = -1). Since 1 
e 0 in the field 
C, the same part (e) gives 1 > 0. Adding, by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), 0 = 1 + (-1) > 0 + 0 = 0. But 0 < 0 is impossible: (O1), with both elements equal to 0, says that exactly one of 0 < 0 and 0 = 0 holds, and 0 = 0 does. So no such relation exists. The proof never asks whether i > 0 or i < 0: part (e) covers both at once. It also never assumes that the hypothetical order agrees with the order of 
R on real numbers. It concludes 1 > 0 and -1 > 0 in whatever order is supposed, and that is the contradiction. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 showed, in an exercise (@fd3:exr-rules-and-absolute-value-c1), that a field containing a square root of -1 cannot be ordered, and named the complex numbers as such a field; the proposition proves that fact for 
C on its own. Compare @fd3:exm-finite-ring-not-orderable, and the integers modulo 3 of Exercise C2 below: there the obstacle to an order is n \cdot 1 = 0 for some n \ge 1. That obstacle is absent here, since n \cdot 1 in 
C is \iota(n \cdot 1), the image of the real number n \cdot 1 > 0 of 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)), which is non-zero as \iota is injective. (The identity n \cdot 1 = \iota(n \cdot 1) is proved by @fd1:ax-induction on n, as for powers in Section 1.1: 0 \cdot 1 = 0 = \iota(0), and if n \cdot 1 = \iota(n \cdot 1), then (n + 1) \cdot 1 = \iota(n \cdot 1) + \iota(1) = \iota((n + 1) \cdot 1) by @prp-reals-embed-complex.) The obstacle in 
C is i^2 = -1 instead. An inequality z < w between complex numbers means nothing: by @prp-complex-not-orderable no order on 
C is compatible with its arithmetic. Apart from arguments that suppose an order on 
C in order to reach a contradiction (the proof above and Exercises B2 and C2), every inequality in this chapter compares real numbers in the order of 
R: moduli, real parts, imaginary parts, or quantities proved to be real, as 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) was in Section 1.3. Writing i > 0 leads, by the proof above, to 0 > 0; so does writing i < 0. Is the following a proof that 
C cannot be ordered? “Every real square is \ge 0, and i^2 = -1 < 0. So i is not a square of anything, a contradiction.” No. The argument proves nothing about orders on 
C. “-1 < 0” is a statement in 
R’s order, and a hypothetical order on 
C need not agree with it on the reals; the argument never even introduces the hypothetical order. And “i is not a square” is false: i = (\pm(1 + i)/\sqrt 2)^2 by @prp-complex-square-roots. The correct proof works inside the supposed order, where i^2 > 0 because i 
e 0. The square-root rule does not survive In 
R, \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{xy} for x, y \ge 0: that is the rule for real square roots used above. A non-zero complex number has two square roots and no preferred one, and no way of preferring one keeps the rule alive. No choice of “the” square root \sqrt{z} of each complex z can satisfy \sqrt{z}\sqrt{w} = \sqrt{zw} for all z, w \in 
C. Whatever is chosen for \sqrt{-1}, it is i or -i (@prp-complex-square-roots (b)), and in both cases \sqrt{-1} \cdot \sqrt{-1} = (\pm i)^2 = -1. But \sqrt{(-1)(-1)} = \sqrt{1}, and the rule itself forces \sqrt{1} = 1: since \sqrt{1} is a square root of 1, 1 = \sqrt{1} \cdot \sqrt{1} = \sqrt{1 \cdot 1} = \sqrt{1}. So the rule would give -1 = 1, which is false in 
C (the real parts -1 < 1 differ). So in this volume the symbol \sqrt{\phantom{x}} is applied only to non-negative reals; for any other z, say “a square root of z” and solve w^2 = z. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. True or false: if z, w \in 
C and z^2 = w^2, then z = w. Justify your answer, and state what is true. 2. Run the formula of @prp-complex-square-roots on z = -4: compute a, b, r, s, x, y and both square roots. 3. Where in the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots is r \ge \abs{a} used? 4. State the idea of the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots in two sentences. (a) False: z = 1, w = -1 have z^2 = w^2 = 1 and z 
e w. What is true: z^2 = w^2 implies z = w or z = -w, since (z - w)(z + w) = z^2 - w^2 = 0 and 
C has no zero divisors (this is the argument of @prp-complex-square-roots (b)). (b) a = -4, b = 0, r = \abs{-4} = 4, s = 1 (as b \ge 0), x = \sqrt{(4 - 4)/2} = 0, y = \sqrt{(4 + 4)/2} = 2. So w = 2i, and the square roots are \pm 2i. (c) To take the square roots at all: r \ge \abs{a} gives r + a \ge 0 and r - a \ge 0, so \sqrt{(r + a)/2} and \sqrt{(r - a)/2} exist. (d) Comparing parts gives x^2 - y^2 = a and 2xy = b; taking moduli gives a third equation x^2 + y^2 = r, and the first and third give x^2 and y^2 by adding and subtracting. The signs are then fixed by 2xy = b, and the absence of zero divisors shows that \pm w are the only roots. B. Practice [B1] 1. Find all w \in 
C with w^2 = -3 + 4i. 2. Hence solve z^2 + 2z + 4 - 4i = 0. (a) Write w = x + yi. Comparing parts, x^2 - y^2 = -3 and xy = 2. Taking moduli (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)), x^2 + y^2 = \abs{-3 + 4i} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5. Adding and subtracting, x^2 = 1 and y^2 = 4. Since xy = 2 > 0, x and y have the same sign, so w = 1 + 2i or w = -1 - 2i, and by @prp-complex-square-roots (b) there are no others. Check: (1 + 2i)^2 = 1 + 4i - 4 = -3 + 4i. (b) By @cor-complex-quadratic-formula with a = 1, b = 2, c = 4 - 4i: the discriminant is 4 - 4(4 - 4i) = -12 + 16i = 4(-3 + 4i), with square root d = 2(1 + 2i) = 2 + 4i by (a), since (2(1 + 2i))^2 = 4(1 + 2i)^2. So z =  rac{-2 + (2 + 4i)}{2} = 2i \qquad 	ext{or} \qquad z =  rac{-2 - (2 + 4i)}{2} = -2 - 2i . Equivalently, completing the square, z^2 + 2z + 4 - 4i = (z + 1)^2 - (-3 + 4i), so z + 1 = \pm(1 + 2i). Check: (2i)^2 + 2(2i) + 4 - 4i = -4 + 4i + 4 - 4i = 0. [B2: Put the proof in order] The nine lines below include the seven lines of a proof of @prp-complex-not-orderable, shuffled, and two lines that do not belong. Write the seven lines in an order that makes a proof, and say what is wrong with each of the other two. 1. i^2 = -1, so -1 > 0. 2. Since i 
e 0, we have i > 0. 3. Suppose < is a relation on 
C that makes 
C an ordered field. 4. 0 < 0 is impossible by (O1), so no such relation exists. 5. So i^2 > 0, because non-zero squares are positive in an ordered field. 6. 1 
e 0, so 1 = 1^2 > 0. 7. i^2 = -1 < 0, because -1 < 0 in 
R. 8. i 
e 0, since i = (0, 1) 
e (0, 0). 9. Adding, 0 = 1 + (-1) > 0 + 0 = 0. An admissible order is (iii), (viii), (v), (i), (vi), (ix), (iv). The constraints are what each line uses: (v), (vi), (i), (ix) and (iv) work in the supposed order, so they come after (iii); (v) also uses (viii); (i) uses (v); (ix) uses (i) and (vi); (iv) uses (ix). Line (viii) is a fact about 
C and uses no order, so it may stand anywhere before (v), even before (iii); line (vi) may stand anywhere after (iii) and before (ix). For instance (iii), (vi), (viii), (v), (i), (ix), (iv) and (viii), (iii), (v), (i), (vi), (ix), (iv) are also admissible. The admissible orders are exactly those that respect these constraints. Line (ii) drops a case: from i 
e 0, trichotomy (O1) gives i > 0 or i < 0, and the line keeps only the first. That is (N7) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, a missing case. Line (v) needs neither case, which is why the proof does not split. Line (vii) cites a reason that is not available: the supposed order on 
C is arbitrary, and nothing says that it agrees with the order of 
R on the real numbers. The proposition is about every relation on 
C, and (vii) quietly replaces “every” by “one that extends 
R’s order”. (The inequality -1 < 0 does hold in any ordered field, by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) applied to 1 > 0, so the line could be repaired by citing that; as written its reason is (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, a fact that is not available.) [B3] Let a, b, c \in 
R with a 
e 0 and b^2 - 4ac < 0. Prove that the equation az^2 + bz + c = 0 has exactly the two solutions z =  rac{-b + i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a} \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad z =  rac{-b - i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a} in 
C, and that they are conjugate to each other. Since 4ac - b^2 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), q \coloneqq \sqrt{4ac - b^2} exists, q > 0, and d \coloneqq iq satisfies d^2 = i^2 q^2 = -(4ac - b^2) = b^2 - 4ac. So @cor-complex-quadratic-formula with this d gives exactly the two solutions displayed, and they are distinct since b^2 - 4ac 
e 0. Since a, b, q are real and 2a 
e 0, the two solutions are - rac{b}{2a} +  rac{q}{2a}\, i \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad - rac{b}{2a} -  rac{q}{2a}\, i , with the same real part and opposite imaginary parts: each is the conjugate of the other (@def-conjugate-modulus). For instance z^2 - 2z + 5 = 0 has b^2 - 4ac = -16, q = 4, and the solutions 1 \pm 2i. C. Going deeper [C1: Find the error] Here is an argument. Claim. For z, w \in 
C, if z^2 = w^2, then z = w or z = -w. Proof. If w = 0, then z^2 = 0, so z = 0 = w, since 
C has no zero divisors. If w 
e 0, put u \coloneqq z/w, which exists because 
C is a field; then u^2 = z^2/w^2 = 1. Taking square roots, u = \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1. In particular, u = 1 or u = -1. Multiplying by w, z = w or z = -w. Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails and the reason, give a counterexample to that line, and repair the argument. The claim is true: it is the argument of @prp-complex-square-roots (b), and it also follows directly from (z - w)(z + w) = z^2 - w^2 = 0 and the absence of zero divisors in 
C. The argument does not prove it. The failing line is “u = \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1”. It uses the rule “u = \sqrt{u^2} whenever u^2 is a non-negative real”, which is neither proved nor true: it is a general “fact” of the kind (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue forbids. The symbol \sqrt{\phantom{x}} is defined only on non-negative reals, and u is a complex number; even for real u, \sqrt{u^2} = \abs{u}, not u. Counterexample to the step: u = -1 has u^2 = 1, but \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1 
e u. The next line, “u = 1 or u = -1”, is a valid weakening of u = 1 (a disjunction follows from either part), so it is not itself an error; it only papers over the loss of the root -1 one line earlier. The rest of the argument (the case w = 0, the division, and multiplying back by w) is correct. Repair: replace the two middle lines by “Then (u - 1)(u + 1) = u^2 - 1 = 0, and 
C has no zero divisors, so u = 1 or u = -1.” Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the claim is true, with a reason. - 3: names the line u = \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1 as the failing one, and its illegal rule u = \sqrt{u^2}. - 2: a counterexample to that step (u = -1, or any u with u^2 = 1, u 
e 1). - 3: a correct repair, by factoring u^2 - 1 and using no zero divisors (or by @prp-complex-square-roots (b) applied to z = 1). Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the claim false; naming the “In particular” line instead of the \sqrt{\phantom{x}} line as the failing one, since it is a valid weakening. [C2: A second proof that there is no order] 1. Use @prp-complex-square-roots to give a second proof of @prp-complex-not-orderable in which the element i is never mentioned. 2. Say why the argument in (a) does not need the special element i. 3. Is the converse of the principle behind (a) true? That is: if a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 admits no order, must -1 be a square in it? Test the ring 
Z/3
Z. [Hint 1] In an ordered field, which elements can be squares? For (c), list the squares of the three classes. (a) Suppose < makes 
C an ordered field. Every square is then \ge 0: a non-zero square is positive by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), and 0^2 = 0. First, -1 
e 0, since otherwise 1 = -(-1) = -0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)), against 1 
e 0 in the field 
C (@thm-complex-numbers-field). By @prp-complex-square-roots (a), applied to the non-zero number -1, some d \in 
C has d^2 = -1. So -1 = d^2 \ge 0, and as -1
