The Unit Circle and Polar Form Addition in 
C is addition of arrows in the plane: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d) puts the second arrow at the tip of the first. Multiplication has a picture too, and Section 1.2 already holds half of it: the modulus of a product is the product of the moduli (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)). The other half is about angles, and angles need the functions cosine and sine, which this volume does not construct. This section first proves everything about directions that needs no angle at all, then states exactly five facts about cosine and sine that it borrows, and from those five builds the polar form of a complex number and the rule “multiply the lengths, add the angles”. Length and direction Every non-zero complex number should be a length times a direction. The length is the modulus. The directions are the complex numbers of length 1, and they deserve a name. The unit circle is the set of complex numbers at distance 1 from 0. We write 
T \coloneqq \{ u \in 
C : \abs{u} = 1 \} for the unit circle. For u = x + yi with x, y \in 
R, the condition \abs{u} = 1 says \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = 1, that is, x^2 + y^2 = 1: both sides of the first equation are non-negative, so it holds exactly when the squares agree (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). So 
T is the circle of radius 1 about 0 in the plane. It contains 1, -1, i and -i, and also 	frac35 + 	frac45 i, since 	frac{9}{25} + 	frac{16}{25} = 1. It does not contain 1 + i, whose modulus is \sqrt 2 
e 1. The next proposition collects what the multiplication of 
C does on 
T. None of it uses an angle. [The Unit Circle] 1. 1 \in 
T. If u, v \in 
T, then uv \in 
T. If u \in 
T, then u 
e 0 and u^{-1} = \conj{u} \in 
T. 2. For every z \in 
C with z 
e 0 there is exactly one pair (r, u) with r \in 
R, r > 0, u \in 
T and z = ru, namely r = \abs{z} and u = z / \abs{z}. 3. For z \in 
C with z 
e 0: 1/z = \conj{z} if and only if \abs{z} = 1. Every part is a statement about moduli, so each follows from the rules of Section 1.2: moduli multiply, u\conj{u} = \abs{u}^2, and only 0 has modulus 0. For (b), divide z by its length; for the uniqueness, take moduli of z = ru. (a) By @prp-modulus-of-real, the modulus of the real number 1 is its absolute value, which is 1; so 1 \in 
T. If \abs{u} = \abs{v} = 1, then \abs{uv} = \abs{u}\abs{v} = 1 by @thm-conjugate-properties (d). Let u \in 
T. Then u 
e 0, since \abs{0} = 0 
e 1 (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)). By @thm-conjugate-properties (c), u \conj{u} = \abs{u}^2 = 1, so \conj{u} satisfies the defining equation of u^{-1}. Since 
C is a field (@thm-complex-numbers-field), inverses are unique (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a)), and u^{-1} = \conj{u}. Finally \abs{\conj{u}} = \abs{u} = 1 by @thm-conjugate-properties (d). (b) Existence. Let r \coloneqq \abs{z}. Then r \ge 0, and r 
e 0 because z 
e 0 (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)); so r > 0, and its inverse r^{-1} is a positive real number (@fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (a)). By @thm-complex-numbers-field the inverse of r in 
C is this real number, so u \coloneqq z / \abs{z} = r^{-1} z is defined, and z = r u. By @thm-conjugate-properties (d) and @prp-modulus-of-real, \abs{u} = \abs{r^{-1}} \abs{z} = r^{-1} r = 1, where \abs{r^{-1}} = r^{-1} because the absolute value of a positive real number is the number itself (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field). So u \in 
T. Uniqueness. Let z = r u with r > 0 and u \in 
T. Taking moduli, \abs{z} = \abs{r} \abs{u} = r \cdot 1 = r, again by @thm-conjugate-properties (d) and @prp-modulus-of-real. Then u = r^{-1} z = z / \abs{z}. So the pair is the one named in the statement. (c) Since inverses are unique, 1/z = \conj{z} holds if and only if z \conj{z} = 1, that is, by @thm-conjugate-properties (c), if and only if \abs{z}^2 = 1 = 1^2. Both \abs{z} and 1 are non-negative, so by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) neither can be strictly smaller than the other, and \abs{z}^2 = 1 holds if and only if \abs{z} = 1. Part (b) is the picture we wanted: z = \abs{z} \cdot u, a length times a direction, and both factors are forced. Part (a) says that the directions are closed under multiplication and inversion and contain 1; Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 3 calls a set with these properties, under an associative product, a group, and 
T is one of its first examples. Part (c) is a practical test: on the unit circle, and only there, dividing by z is the same as conjugating. Write z = 3 + 4i as r u with r > 0 and u \in 
T. What is 1/u? By @prp-unit-circle (b), r = \abs{3 + 4i} = 5 and u = 	frac35 + 	frac45 i. By (a), 1/u = \conj{u} = 	frac35 - 	frac45 i. Check:  ig(	frac35 + 	frac45 i ig) ig(	frac35 - 	frac45 i ig) = 	frac{9}{25} + 	frac{16}{25} = 1. So far a direction is a point u of 
T, and multiplying two directions gives a third. What we cannot yet say is how much a direction turns the plane. For that we need to measure positions on the circle by a real number, an angle, so that multiplying directions adds angles. That is a job for cosine and sine. What this volume borrows about cosine and sine An angle should be a real number 	heta that walks around the circle: a point (\cos	heta, \sin	heta) on 
T, moving as 	heta moves, returning to its start after a full turn of length 2\pi. Defining such functions needs limits of functions, by power series or by integrals. This volume develops no limits of functions, so it does not define cosine and sine. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 10 does: there \cos and \sin are defined by power series, \pi is defined as twice the least positive zero of \cos, and the facts below are proved. Its 
R is a complete ordered field, so by @fd3:thm-cof-uniqueness it is our 
R, up to the one order-preserving field isomorphism; the functions and the number carry over along it. We write 2\pi
Z \coloneqq \{ 2\pi k : k \in 
Z \}, the integer multiples of 2\pi in 
R. What This Volume Borrows about Cosine and Sine There are functions \cos, \sin \colon 
R 	o 
R and a real number \pi > 0 with the following properties. They are assumed here and proved in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 10. 1. \cos^2	heta + \sin^2	heta = 1 for every 	heta \in 
R. 2. For all 	heta, \varphi \in 
R,  egin{aligned} \cos(	heta + \varphi) &= \cos	heta \cos\varphi - \sin	heta \sin\varphi , \ \sin(	heta + \varphi) &= \sin	heta \cos\varphi + \cos	heta \sin\varphi . \end{aligned} 3. For 	heta \in 
R: \cos	heta = 1 if and only if 	heta \in 2\pi
Z. 4. For every (x, y) \in 
R^2 with x^2 + y^2 = 1 there is 	heta \in 
R with \cos	heta = x and \sin	heta = y. 5. \sin	heta > 0 whenever 0 < 	heta < \pi. In words: (T1) puts the point (\cos	heta, \sin	heta) on the unit circle; (T2) is the pair of addition formulas; (T3) says that the cosine reaches 1 exactly at the multiples of a full turn; (T4) says that every point of the circle is reached; (T5) says that during the first half turn the point stays in the upper half plane. This box is where the chapter borrows. Like @fd1:ax-induction, which Logic and Proof assumed and Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1 proved, it is a statement assumed in one volume and proved in another. Nothing in Sections 1.1–1.4, and nothing in this section above the box, uses it. From here on we use these five facts about \cos, \sin and \pi and no others: no value such as \cos(\pi/3) = 	frac12, no periodicity, no picture of a graph. Whatever else we need, we derive, and each proof that uses one of the facts names it by its number. Two consequences come at once. - \cos 0 = 1, by (T3), since 0 = 2\pi \cdot 0 \in 2\pi
Z. Then (T1) gives \sin^2 0 = 1 - 1 = 0, so \sin 0 = 0, because a non-zero real number has a positive square (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). - \cos(2\pi k) = 1 and \sin(2\pi k) = 0 for every k \in 
Z, by (T3) and then (T1) in the same way. The five facts are about \cos, \sin and \pi only. A school fact such as \sin(\pi/6) = 	frac12 is not among them, and a proof in this volume may not quote it: @exm-special-angles below derives the few values we use. Nor do the facts say that \cos and \sin are “periodic with period 2\pi” as functions; that is true, and derivable from (T2) and (T3), but no proof here needs it. Polar form With angles available, we can name the point of 
T at angle 	heta. e^{i	heta} is the point of the unit circle at angle 	heta. Polar Form For 	heta \in 
R we write e^{i	heta} \coloneqq \cos	heta + i \sin	heta . Let z \in 
C with z 
e 0. A polar form of z is an expression z = r e^{i	heta} with r \in 
R, r > 0, and 	heta \in 
R. Then 	heta is an argument of z. In words: the first line is an abbreviation, not an exponential. This volume has no exponential function, the letter e on its own means nothing here, and the only rule of exponents we will use for e^{i	heta} is the one proved below (@thm-polar-multiplication (a)). Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 10 shows that e^{i	heta} is indeed the value of the complex exponential function at i	heta; the notation anticipates that, and the linear algebra volumes write their roots of unity with it. The exponent may be written in any form equal to i	heta with 	heta real, and the symbol then means e^{i	heta}: for example e^{-i	heta} = e^{i(-	heta)}, e^{2\pi i} = e^{i \cdot 2\pi}, e^{in	heta} = e^{i(n	heta)} and e^{-2\pi i} = e^{i(-2\pi)}. This is unambiguous, because the real number 	heta is determined by i	heta (it is its imaginary part). The second part asks for a positive real r and allows any real 	heta. The point e^{i	heta} lies on 
T. Indeed \abs{e^{i	heta}} = \sqrt{\cos^2	heta + \sin^2	heta} = \sqrt 1 = 1, by @def-conjugate-modulus and (T1). So r e^{i	heta} is a length r times a direction, as in @prp-unit-circle (b), and that proposition gives r = \abs{z} for every polar form of z. Examples. - e^{i0} = \cos 0 + i \sin 0 = 1, by the consequences of the box. So 1 = 1 \cdot e^{i0} and 5 = 5 e^{i0} are polar forms. - e^{2\pi i} = \cos 2\pi + i \sin 2\pi = 1, by the second consequence with k = 1. So 1 = 1 \cdot e^{2\pi i} as well: 0 and 2\pi are both arguments of 1, and they differ, since \pi > 0. - The number 0 has no polar form, since \abs{r e^{i	heta}} = r > 0. A non-example by minimal change. Allow r < 0: then -1 = (-1) \cdot e^{i0} looks like a polar form of -1 with argument 0. The clause that fails is r > 0, and it matters: with negative r allowed, the length could no longer be read off as \abs{z}, and 1 = 1 \cdot e^{i0} and -1 = (-1) e^{i0} would share the argument 0. We will see in @exm-special-angles that -1 = 1 \cdot e^{i\pi} is a genuine polar form. The examples already show why the definition says an argument: 1 = e^{i0} = e^{2\pi i}. How much freedom there is, exactly, is part (b) of @prp-polar-form below. First, the reason for the notation: these numbers multiply the way exponentials do. [Multiplication in Polar Form] 1. e^{i	heta} e^{i\varphi} = e^{i(	heta + \varphi)} for all 	heta, \varphi \in 
R. 2. e^{i0} = 1, and (e^{i	heta})^{-1} = e^{-i	heta} = \conj{e^{i	heta}} for every 	heta \in 
R. 3. If r, s \in 
R with r, s > 0 and 	heta, \varphi \in 
R, then (r e^{i	heta})(s e^{i\varphi}) = rs \, e^{i(	heta + \varphi)}, and this is a polar form of the product. Multiply out (\cos	heta + i\sin	heta)(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi) with the rule of @def-complex-numbers: the real and imaginary parts that appear are exactly the right-hand sides of the addition formulas (T2). The rest is bookkeeping with inverses and moduli. (a) By the multiplication rule of @def-complex-numbers,  egin{aligned} e^{i	heta} e^{i\varphi} &= (\cos	heta\cos\varphi - \sin	heta\sin\varphi) + (\cos	heta\sin\varphi + \sin	heta\cos\varphi) i \ &= \cos(	heta + \varphi) + i \sin(	heta + \varphi) , \end{aligned} where the second equality is (T2), with the two products in the imaginary part reordered by commutativity in 
R. The right-hand side is e^{i(	heta + \varphi)}. (b) e^{i0} = 1 was shown in the first example above. By (a) with \varphi = -	heta, e^{i	heta} e^{-i	heta} = e^{i0} = 1, so e^{-i	heta} is the inverse of e^{i	heta}, by uniqueness of inverses in the field 
C (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). Since e^{i	heta} \in 
T, its inverse is also its conjugate (@prp-unit-circle (a)). (c) By @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws (commutativity and associativity of \cdot), (r e^{i	heta})(s e^{i\varphi}) = (rs)(e^{i	heta} e^{i\varphi}), and (a) turns this into rs \, e^{i(	heta + \varphi)}. Here rs > 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (multiply 0 < r by s > 0), so this is a polar form. In words: to multiply two complex numbers, multiply their moduli and add their arguments. This is the chapter’s third named move, multiply moduli, add angles. Multiplying by a fixed w = s e^{i\varphi} therefore turns the plane about 0 by the angle \varphi and stretches it by the factor s. The picture shows z, w and zw for \abs{z} = 1.5, \abs{w} = 1.2, and arguments of 20^\circ and 50^\circ (a full turn being 360^\circ, that is, 2\pi). The arrow for zw has length 1.5 	imes 1.2 = 1.8 and makes the angle 20^\circ + 50^\circ = 70^\circ with the positive real axis: it is the arrow for z, turned by the argument of w and stretched by the modulus of w. The small arc marks the argument of z, the large arc the extra turn by the argument of w, and the dashed arc is part of the unit circle, where the numbers e^{i	heta} live. Now the freedom in the argument. Every non-zero number has a polar form, and its arguments are determined up to a whole number of full turns. [Existence and Uniqueness of Polar Form] 1. Every z \in 
C with z 
e 0 has a polar form, and every polar form z = r e^{i	heta} has r = \abs{z}. 2. For r, s \in 
R with r, s > 0 and 	heta, \varphi \in 
R, r e^{i	heta} = s e^{i\varphi} \iff r = s 	ext{ and } 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z . (a) By @prp-unit-circle (b), z = \abs{z} \cdot u with u = x + yi \in 
T, so x^2 + y^2 = 1. By (T4) there is 	heta \in 
R with \cos	heta = x and \sin	heta = y, that is, u = e^{i	heta}. Hence z = \abs{z} e^{i	heta}, with \abs{z} > 0. Conversely, if z = r e^{i	heta} is a polar form, then e^{i	heta} \in 
T, and the uniqueness in @prp-unit-circle (b) gives r = \abs{z}. (b) Suppose first that r e^{i	heta} = s e^{i\varphi}. The number r e^{i	heta} is non-zero: r 
e 0, e^{i	heta} \in 
T is non-zero (@prp-unit-circle (a)), and a product of non-zero elements of the field 
C is non-zero (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)). So both sides are polar forms of the same non-zero number, and r = s by (a). Multiplying by r^{-1} gives e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi}. In the other direction, if r = s, the two sides are equal exactly when e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi}. So it remains to show that e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} if and only if 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z. Multiplying by e^{-i\varphi}, and back by e^{i\varphi}, shows that e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} holds if and only if e^{i	heta} e^{-i\varphi} = e^{i\varphi} e^{-i\varphi}, that is, by @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and (b), if and only if e^{i(	heta - \varphi)} = 1. Comparing real and imaginary parts, this says \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1 and \sin(	heta - \varphi) = 0. The second condition follows from the first: by (T1), \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1 gives \sin^2(	heta - \varphi) = 0, hence \sin(	heta - \varphi) = 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} if and only if \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1, and by (T3) that holds if and only if 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z. Existence came from (T4), and uniqueness from (T3), with (T1) helping and (T2) entering through @thm-polar-multiplication. “Comparing arguments” therefore always means comparing them up to a multiple of 2\pi, and the next warning is the trap this sets. From e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} one may not conclude 	heta = \varphi: e^{i0} = e^{2\pi i} = 1, and 0 
e 2\pi. Only 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z follows (@prp-polar-form (b)). Forgetting this loses solutions as soon as an equation is solved for an angle; Section 1.6 meets an equation where it would lose all but one of them. Powers Repeating @thm-polar-multiplication gives powers. The powers z^n are those of the recursion z^0 = 1, z^{n+1} = z^n z (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring). [De Moivre’s Formula] For every 	heta \in 
R and every n \in 
N,  igl(e^{i	heta} igr)^n = e^{in	heta} , \quad 	ext{that is,} \quad (\cos	heta + i\sin	heta)^n = \cos n	heta + i \sin n	heta . Consequently (r e^{i	heta})^n = r^n e^{in	heta} for every real r > 0, and this is a polar form. A power is a repeated product, and each new factor e^{i	heta} adds 	heta to the argument, by @thm-polar-multiplication (a). So induction on n, along the recursion z^{n+1} = z^n z. We use @fd1:ax-induction on n, read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b); here n	heta is the product in 
R of n \cdot 1_{
R} and 	heta (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a)). For n = 0, the left side is (e^{i	heta})^0 = 1 by the recursion, and the right side is e^{i0} = 1 by @thm-polar-multiplication (b). Suppose (e^{i	heta})^n = e^{in	heta} for some n \in 
N. Then  igl(e^{i	heta} igr)^{n+1} =  igl(e^{i	heta} igr)^n e^{i	heta} = e^{in	heta} e^{i	heta} = e^{i(n	heta + 	heta)} = e^{i(n+1)	heta} , by the recursion, the induction hypothesis, @thm-polar-multiplication (a), and (n + 1) \cdot 1_{
R} = n \cdot 1_{
R} + 1_{
R} (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a)) with distributivity in 
R. This proves the formula for every n \in 
N. For the consequence, @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (c) gives (r e^{i	heta})^n = r^n (e^{i	heta})^n = r^n e^{in	heta}. The power r^n is the same whether it is computed in 
R or in 
C, by the remark after @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring in Section 1.1, and r^n > 0 because a product of positive reals is positive (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c); induction on n, with r^0 = 1 > 0). For a negative exponent, Exercise C1 below defines z^{-n} locally and proves the matching formula; nothing in the text uses it. The five borrowed facts give no particular value of \cos or \sin except at multiples of 2\pi. Every other value this chapter uses is derived next, from (T1)–(T5) and the algebra of Sections 1.1–1.4. [Special Angles] Show, using only (T1)–(T5) and the results proved so far, that  egin{aligned} &e^{i\pi} = -1, \qquad e^{i\pi/2} = i, \qquad e^{i\pi/3} = 	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i, \ &e^{i\pi/6} = 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} + 	frac12 i, \qquad e^{i\pi/4} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} + 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} i . \end{aligned} Each value is found the same way: a power of the unknown point is a point we already know, and (T5) chooses between the candidates. Since \pi > 0, each of \pi/2, \pi/3, \pi/4, \pi/6 lies strictly between 0 and \pi, so (T5) gives \operatorname{Im} e^{i	heta} = \sin	heta > 0 for each of them. (i) e^{i\pi} = -1. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi}. By @thm-de-moivre, u^2 = e^{2\pi i} = 1, so (u - 1)(u + 1) = u^2 - 1 = 0, and since 
C has no zero divisors (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)), u = 1 or u = -1. Suppose u = 1. Then \cos\pi = 1, so \pi = 2\pi k for some k \in 
Z by (T3); dividing by \pi 
e 0 gives 1 = 2k in 
R, an equation between images of integers. The embedding of 
Z into 
R, through 
Q (@fd3:prp-integers-embed-rationals) and \kappa (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), is injective and preserves + and \cdot, so 1 = 2k holds in 
Z. But 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd, and an odd integer is not of the form 2k (@fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a)). So u 
e 1, and e^{i\pi} = -1. (ii) e^{i\pi/2} = i. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi/2}. By @thm-polar-multiplication (a), u^2 = e^{i\pi} = -1 = i^2, so (u - i)(u + i) = 0 and u = \pm i. Since \operatorname{Im} u > 0 and \operatorname{Im}(-i) = -1 < 0, u = i. (iii) e^{i\pi/3} = 	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi/3}. By @thm-de-moivre, u^3 = e^{i\pi} = -1. Multiplying out shows (u + 1)(u^2 - u + 1) = u^3 + 1 = 0. Now u 
e -1, since \operatorname{Im} u > 0; so u^2 - u + 1 = 0. By @cor-complex-quadratic-formula with a = 1, b = -1, c = 1, and d \coloneqq \sqrt 3\, i, a square root of b^2 - 4ac = -3 (indeed (\sqrt 3\, i)^2 = 3 i^2 = -3), u =  rac{1 + \sqrt 3\, i}{2} \quad 	ext{or} \quad u =  rac{1 - \sqrt 3\, i}{2} . Since \operatorname{Im} u > 0, u = 	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i. (iv) e^{i\pi/6} = 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} + 	frac12 i. Since \pi/6 = \pi/2 + (-\pi/3), @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and (b) give e^{i\pi/6} = e^{i\pi/2} e^{-i\pi/3} = i \cdot \conj{e^{i\pi/3}} = i \Bigl(  rac12 -  rac{\sqrt 3}{2} i \Bigr) =  rac{\sqrt 3}{2} +  rac12 i , by (ii) and (iii). (v) e^{i\pi/4} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} + 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} i. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi/4}. By @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and (ii), u^2 = e^{i\pi/2} = i. The formula of @prp-complex-square-roots for z = i (so a = 0, b = 1, r = \abs{i} = 1) gives the square root w = \sqrt{1/2} + \sqrt{1/2}\, i, and \sqrt{1/2} = 1/\sqrt 2, since both are non-negative and square to 	frac12. title: 1.6 Higher Roots, Roots of Unity, and a Look Ahead
content:
Higher Roots, Roots of Unity, and a Look Ahead Section 1.4 solved z^2 = c with real square roots alone. Polar form turns the general equation z^n = c into a question about lengths and angles: by De Moivre’s formula (@thm-de-moivre), raising to the n-th power raises the modulus to the n-th power and multiplies the argument by n. The angle part is a linear equation for a real number, with the ambiguity 2\pi
Z of @prp-polar-form attached. The length part is the real equation r^n = ho with ho > 0, and before anything else we must know that it has exactly one positive solution. This section proves that, solves z^n = c, counts the solutions, studies the case c = 1, and ends with a look ahead at polynomial equations in general. Real n-th roots For n = 2, Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 6 built the square root by the move construct a point as a supremum (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), and an exercise there ran the same move for cube roots (@fd3:exr-measuring-by-rationals-b2). For a general exponent the move is the same; only the estimate for (s + h)^n needs a new tool, and @lem-difference-of-powers supplies it. Here n \cdot 1_{
R} is written n, and powers in 
R are those of @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring with R = 
R, the same recursion as @fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). Real n-th Roots Let n \in 
N with n \ge 1. 1. If s, t \in 
R and 0 \le s < t, then s^n < t^n. 2. For every a \in 
R with a \ge 0 there is exactly one b \in 
R with b \ge 0 and b^n = a. We write \sqrt[n]{a} \coloneqq b. For n = 2 it is the square root \sqrt a of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. Part (a) is the factorization t^n - s^n = (t - s)(t^{n-1} + t^{n-2}s + \dots + s^{n-1}): both factors are positive. For (b), let s be the supremum of the set S of non-negative y with y^n \le a, and rule out s^n < a and s^n > a. If s^n < a, we want h > 0 with (s + h)^n \le a. Working backwards: for 0 < h \le 1, the same factorization writes (s + h)^n - s^n as h times a sum of n terms, each at most (s + 1)^{n-1}. So (s + h)^n - s^n \le h \cdot n(s + 1)^{n-1}, and it is enough that this be at most half the room a - s^n. That gives h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^n)/(2n(s + 1)^{n-1})\}. If s^n > a, we want h > 0 with (s - h)^n \ge a still, which makes s - h a smaller upper bound. Now s^n - (s - h)^n \le h \cdot n s^{n-1}, and it is enough that this equal the excess s^n - a. That gives h \coloneqq (s^n - a)/(n s^{n-1}). Three facts are used throughout: a power of a non-negative real number is non-negative and a power of a positive one is positive (induction on the exponent with @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)); if 0 \le y \le 1 then y^k \le y for every k \ge 1, while if y \ge 1 then y^k \ge y (induction: y^{k+1} = y^k y, and @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) or equality); and if 0 \le x \le x' and 0 \le y \le y', then xy \le x'y \le x'y' (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) twice, or equality). (a) By @lem-difference-of-powers in the commutative ring 
R, t^n - s^n = (t - s) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k s^{n-1-k} . Every term of the sum is \ge 0, and the term with k = n - 1 is t^{n-1} > 0, since t > s \ge 0. So the sum is \ge t^{n-1} > 0. Also t - s > 0. Hence t^n - s^n > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). (b) Uniqueness. If b, c \ge 0 and b 
e c, say b < c, then b^n < c^n by (a); so at most one non-negative b has b^n = a. Existence. If a = 0, then b \coloneqq 0 works, since 0^n = 0^{n-1} \cdot 0 = 0. Let a > 0, and let S \coloneqq \{ y \in 
R : y \ge 0 	ext{ and } y^n \le a \} . Put m \coloneqq \min\{1, a\} > 0. Since 0 < m \le 1, m^n \le m \le a, so m \in S. Put M \coloneqq \max\{1, a\}. If y > M, then y > 1, so y^n \ge y > M \ge a and y 
otin S; hence M is an upper bound of S. Since 
R is a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:def-complete-ordered-field), S has a supremum; let s \coloneqq \sup S. Then s \ge m > 0. Case s^n < a. Let h \coloneqq \min\Bigl\{ 1,  rac{a - s^n}{2n(s + 1)^{n-1}} \Bigr\} . It depends only on a, n and s, and h > 0, since a - s^n > 0 and 2n(s + 1)^{n-1} > 0. By @lem-difference-of-powers, (s + h)^n - s^n = h \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (s + h)^k s^{n-1-k} . Since 0 \le s < s + h \le s + 1, each term satisfies (s + h)^k s^{n-1-k} \le (s + 1)^k (s + 1)^{n-1-k} = (s + 1)^{n-1}, by (a) (or equality), the third fact, and @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a). A sum of n terms, each at most (s + 1)^{n-1}, is at most n (s + 1)^{n-1}. Hence (s + h)^n \le s^n + h \cdot n(s + 1)^{n-1} \le s^n +  rac{a - s^n}{2} < a . So s + h \in S, and s + h > s, against s being an upper bound of S. Case s^n > a. Let h \coloneqq  rac{s^n - a}{n s^{n-1}} , which depends only on a, n and s, and is positive. Since a > 0, we have s^n - a < s^n \le n s^n, so h < s^n/(n s^{n-1}) = s/n \le s; thus 0 < s - h < s. By @lem-difference-of-powers and the same bound, with 0 < s - h < s, each of the n terms of \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} s^k (s - h)^{n-1-k} is at most s^{n-1}, so s^n - (s - h)^n \le h \cdot n s^{n-1} = s^n - a , that is, (s - h)^n \ge a. Now let y \in S. If y > s - h, then (a) gives y^n > (s - h)^n \ge a, against y \in S. So y \le s - h, and s - h is an upper bound of S smaller than s, against s being the least upper bound. Both cases are impossible, so s^n = a by trichotomy, and b \coloneqq s \ge 0 works. For n = 2, the number \sqrt[2]{a} is non-negative and squares to a, so it is \sqrt a, by the uniqueness in @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. The constants were found backwards in the Idea and placed first in the proof, and each depends on a, n and s only. Completeness was used once, to produce s. For a > 0 the root is positive, since 0^n = 0 
e a. For instance \sqrt[3]{8} = 2 and \sqrt[4]{4} = \sqrt 2, since 2^3 = 8 and (\sqrt 2)^4 =  igl((\sqrt 2)^2 igr)^2 = 4, and both are non-negative. The symbol \sqrt[n]{a} is used only for non-negative real a; the next theorem shows why it could not mean “the” n-th root of a complex number. Solving the equation z to the n equals c Now the main result. Every non-zero complex number has exactly n different n-th roots, and polar form lists them. [n-th Roots of a Complex Number] Let n \in 
N with n \ge 1, and let c \in 
C with c 
e 0. Let c = ho e^{i\alpha} be a polar form of c (@prp-polar-form), and for k \in 
Z put z_k \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{ho} \; e^{i(\alpha + 2\pi k)/n} . 1. For z \in 
C: z^n = c if and only if z = z_k for some k \in 
Z. 2. For k, l \in 
Z: z_k = z_l if and only if n \mid k - l (@fd2:def-divides). 3. The map \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\} 	o \{ z \in 
C : z^n = c \}, k \mapsto z_k, is a bijection. So c has exactly n n-th roots (@fd2:def-finite). In particular every non-zero complex number has an n-th root, and every u \in 
T has one in 
T. Write the unknown in polar form, z = r e^{i	heta}. De Moivre turns z^n = c into r^n e^{in	heta} = ho e^{i\alpha}, and the uniqueness half of polar form splits that into a real equation for the length, r^n = ho, and an equation for the angle, n	heta \in \alpha + 2\pi
Z. The first has one solution, r = \sqrt[n]{ho}. The second has the solutions 	heta = (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n, one for each integer k. Different k can give the same point, and they do exactly when the angles differ by a whole number of turns, that is, when n \mid k - l. So the k that matter are the remainders 0, \dots, n - 1. Before reading on: where is the uniqueness half of the polar form used, and where the uniqueness of the real n-th root? Here ho = \abs{c} > 0 by @prp-polar-form (a), so \sqrt[n]{ho} > 0 exists by @lem-reals-nth-root (b). (a) Let z \in 
C. If z = 0, then z^n = 0^{n-1} \cdot 0 = 0 
e c (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), and z is no z_k, since every z_k has modulus \sqrt[n]{ho} > 0. So let z 
e 0, and fix a polar form z = r e^{i	heta} (@prp-polar-form (a)). By @thm-de-moivre, z^n = r^n e^{in	heta}, a polar form with r^n > 0. By @prp-polar-form (b), z^n = c \iff r^n = ho \ 	ext{ and } \ n	heta - \alpha \in 2\pi
Z . Since r > 0, the uniqueness in @lem-reals-nth-root (b) gives r^n = ho \iff r = \sqrt[n]{ho}. And n	heta - \alpha = 2\pi k holds for a given k \in 
Z exactly when 	heta = (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n. (\Rightarrow) If z^n = c, then r = \sqrt[n]{ho} and 	heta = (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n for some k \in 
Z, so z = z_k. (\Leftarrow) If z = z_k, use the polar form r \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{ho}, 	heta \coloneqq (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n of z in the equivalence above. Both conditions on the right hold, so z^n = c. (b) The numbers z_k and z_l are given in polar form with the same modulus. By @prp-polar-form (b), z_k = z_l if and only if  rac{\alpha + 2\pi k}{n} -  rac{\alpha + 2\pi l}{n} =  rac{2\pi (k - l)}{n} \in 2\pi
Z , that is, if and only if 2\pi(k - l)/n = 2\pi m for some m \in 
Z. Multiplying by n/(2\pi), and back, this says k - l = mn, an equation between integers. So z_k = z_l if and only if n \mid k - l. (c) By (a), each z_k is a solution, so the map is into the set of solutions. Injective: let 0 \le l < k \le n - 1. Then 0 < k - l < n. If z_k = z_l, then n \mid k - l by (b), and since n > 0 and k - l > 0, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) gives n \le k - l, a contradiction. So z_k 
e z_l. Surjective: let z^n = c. By (a), z = z_k for some k \in 
Z. Division with remainder (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a)) gives k = qn + j with q \in 
Z and 0 \le j \le n - 1. Then n \mid k - j, so z = z_k = z_j by (b). Hence the map is a bijection. Composing it with the bijection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \{0, \dots, n - 1\}, j \mapsto j - 1, shows that the set of solutions has n elements (@fd2:def-finite). Finally, z_0 is an n-th root of c. If \abs{c} = 1, then ho = 1 and \sqrt[n]{1} = 1, since 1 \ge 0 and 1^n = 1; so every z_k has modulus 1 and lies in 
T. By @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{x}^2 = x^2, \abs{y}^2 = y^2, \abs{x + y}^2 = (x + y)^2 and \abs{x}\abs{y} = \abs{xy}. Hence (\abs{x} + \abs{y})^2 - \abs{x + y}^2 = \abs{x}^2 + 2\abs{x}\abs{y} + \abs{y}^2 - x^2 - 2xy - y^2 = 2 igl(\abs{xy} - xy igr) \ge 0 , since xy \le \abs{xy} (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c)). So \abs{x + y}^2 \le (\abs{x} + \abs{y})^2. If \abs{x + y} > \abs{x} + \abs{y}, then @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), applied to these non-negative elements, would give \abs{x + y}^2 > (\abs{x} + \abs{y})^2; so \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. (b) The trapping proof (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), proved from (c)) uses -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}: it compares x itself with real numbers. For a complex x that is not real such a comparison means nothing, since no order on 
C is compatible with its arithmetic (@prp-complex-not-orderable). The squaring proof of (a) is the one that survives: in the complex triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) the cross term 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) is bounded by a comparison between real numbers, \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} (@lem-real-part-at-most-modulus), which replaces xy \le \abs{xy} here. [R4] Find all z \in 
C with \conj{z} = z^2. The tool: take moduli first. If \conj{z} = z^2, then \abs{z} = \abs{\conj{z}} = \abs{z^2} = \abs{z}^2 (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)), so \abs{z} igl(\abs{z} - 1 igr) = 0 and \abs{z} = 0 or \abs{z} = 1. If \abs{z} = 0, then z = 0 (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)), and z = 0 is a solution. If \abs{z} = 1, multiply \conj{z} = z^2 by z: 1 = z\conj{z} = z^3 (@thm-conjugate-properties (c)). So z is a cube root of unity: z = 1 or z = -	frac12 \pm 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i (the Check above). Conversely, each cube root of unity \zeta lies in 
T (Exercise B3), so \conj{\zeta} = \zeta^{-1} (@prp-unit-circle (a)), and \zeta^{-1} = \zeta^2 because \zeta \cdot \zeta^2 = \zeta^3 = 1. So each is a solution. The solutions are 0, 1, -	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i and -	frac12 - 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i. Why the look-alike tools are worse. Comparing real and imaginary parts, with z = x + yi, gives x^2 - y^2 = x and 2xy = -y, which can be solved, but only with a case split by hand (y = 0 or x = -	frac12). “Divide \conj{z} = z^2 by z” silently loses the solution z = 0. Polar form works, but it is not needed: the moduli settle \abs{z}, and the cube roots of unity can be found without angles, as in the Check.
